intro.title: Tranche
intro.sub: PayPal invoice tranches drive a Bryntum delivery plan. An AI agent proposes; a human approves.
intro.note: Draft render. PayPal runs as a deterministic, sandbox-shaped mock in this video.

outro.title: Thanks for watching
outro.sub: npm install && npm start — then open the board on port 4317.
outro.note: This draft uses mock PayPal. A sandbox Invoicing v2 client is built and unit-tested against a local stub, but has not yet run against the real PayPal sandbox. Bryntum Gantt and SchedulerPro trial, watermark left visible. Repository link: on the Devpost page.

steps.text: Freelancers and small agencies get paid in tranches. Tranche turns every PayPal invoice into a milestone on a Bryntum Gantt, and each delivery phase depends on the payment before it.
Acme's second invoice is nine days overdue, so the build phase it unlocks is blocked, in red. The team capacity view below is a Bryntum Scheduler Pro on the same project, so bookings follow the plan.
Invoice two for Acme is nine days overdue. What does that do to the plan? Draft a reminder too.
Invoice INV-2 for Acme is 9 days overdue. What does that do to the plan? Draft a reminder too.
The agent runs on the GitHub Copilot SDK. Its tools can read the board and file requests, but they cannot change anything. And it never does date maths: it asks our scheduler for a preview.
The dashed ghost bars are that preview. The phases behind invoice two slide, and the banner says how far Acme's delivery slips. Nothing has moved yet.
The agent filed two requests: apply the new dates, and send a PayPal reminder with a friendly note. Each card is bound to its preview and a payload hash, and only the owner can approve.
Apply runs inside the Bryntum engine as one transaction. The browser reports the engine's dates back, and the server checks every one of them.
Changed my mind? Undo reverts it through Bryntum's state tracking manager, and the plan is back where it was.
Now the client pays. PayPal is a mock in this draft, so a demo button plays the payer.
The paid event arrives, and the reminder I never sent turns stale. It can't be approved any more, so nobody nags a client who just paid.
The payment event also wakes the agent by itself. It proposes moving the plan to the real payment date.
One click, and the build phase now starts on the day the money arrived.
Every request, approval, apply, undo and PayPal event lands in the audit log.

The top bar says exactly what is running: PayPal is a mock in this draft, and the agent is a live model through the GitHub Copilot SDK. Judges can bring their own key, or use the clearly labelled scripted agent.
Tranche: PayPal payments that move the plan, with a human in the loop.
